title: Accents of English
desc: Listen to the same language in six accents and learn typical local words.
intro: English sounds different around the world. Listen first, answer the questions, and then read the script. The voice comes from your device, so some details of each accent may sound similar.

sets.title: At the coffee shop
sets.intro: Listen to a customer and a cashier in an American coffee shop. Notice the words apartment, elevator and parking lot.
notes: The r is pronounced in every position: car = /kɑːr/, water = /ˈwɔːtər/.
A t between vowels often sounds like a quick d: city, water, better.
Words like bath and dance use a short /æ/ sound.
Typical words: apartment (flat), elevator (lift), line (queue), check (bill), parking lot (car park).
Speakers often join words in fast speech: gonna, wanna, gotta.

lines.text: Hi, can I get a large coffee to go?
Sure. Would you like cream or sugar?
Just a little cream, please. And one blueberry muffin.
That's six dollars and fifty cents. You can pay at the register.
Here's my card. Is there a parking lot near here?
Yes, it's behind the building. It's free for the first hour.
Great. I'm moving into a new apartment this weekend.
Nice! Is it on a high floor? The elevator in my building is always broken.
No, it's on the second floor, so I can take the stairs.
Good luck with the move. Have a nice day!

sets.title: At the car rental counter
sets.intro: Jake picks up a rental car in the United States. Listen for American words for cars and roads.
notes: The r in "car", "driver" and "tour" is strong and clear.
"License" has a quick, light ending: /ˈlaɪsəns/.
The t in "water" and "better" sounds like a quick d.
Americans say "gas" for fuel and "trunk" for the back of a car.

lines.text: Good morning. Welcome to Sunset Car Rental. How can I help you?
Hi. I have a reservation for a compact car under the name Jake Morris.
Let me check. Yes, here it is. Can I see your driver's license, please?
Sure, here you go.
Thanks. Would you like to add insurance for twenty dollars a day?
No, thanks. My credit card already covers that.
Okay. The car comes with a full tank of gas, so please bring it back full.
No problem. Is there any limit on the mileage?
No, it's unlimited. Just remember that some highways have tolls, so keep some cash.
Good idea. Where can I put my bags? Is the trunk big enough?
It's pretty big. You can fit two large suitcases in there.
Perfect. Thanks for your help!
You're welcome. Have a safe trip, and stop at a rest stop if you get tired.

notes: The vowel in "baseball" and "game" glides like "ay-ee".

lines.text: Can you believe we got seats behind home plate?

Don't worry. It's pretty simple. The pitcher throws the ball and the batter tries to hit it.
Okay. How many innings are there?
Nine, usually. A game can take about three hours.
Three hours! I'd better get a snack. Do you want a hot dog?
Sure, and a soda, too. I'll grab the napkins.
Which team are you rooting for?
The home team, of course. I've been a fan since I was a kid.
Then I'll root for them too. Oh, look, the crowd is standing up!
It's the seventh inning stretch. Everybody stands up and sings a song.
That's a fun tradition. I'm having a great time!

lines.text: Morning, Sophie. Shall we have a look at the flat?

Is it near the tube? I'd rather not drive.
Ten minutes on foot. The shops are just round the corner too.
Brilliant. What about the rubbish? Where do I put the bins?
The bins are at the back, and they're collected on Tuesdays.
Cheers. Can I move in at the end of the month?

British speakers say "ten past nine" for 9:10 and "half past nine" for 9:30.
"Chemist" is a shop where you get medicine.
Polite phrases like "Would that suit you?" are common.

lines.text: Good morning, Riverside Surgery. How can I help?
Hello, I'd like to make an appointment to see the doctor, please. I've had a bad cough for a week.
Let me see. Are you registered with a GP here?
Yes, I'm registered with Doctor Patel.
I can offer you tomorrow at twenty past nine. Would that suit you?
That's perfect. I'm feeling a bit under the weather and I've got a temperature too.
I'm sorry to hear that. Please bring a list of any medicine you take.
Will the doctor give me a prescription?
Possibly. If so, you can collect it from the chemist round the corner.
And I'll need a sick note for work, I think.
The doctor can sort that out for you. Please arrive ten minutes early.
Will do. Thanks very much. Cheers!

sets.title: A broken boiler
sets.intro: Megan phones her landlord about a problem in her flat. Listen for polite British phrases.
notes: "I'm afraid..." is a polite way to give bad news.
"Oh dear" is a mild reaction to a problem.
The r is not pronounced at the end of "radiator" or "plumber".
"Lovely" and "brilliant" show that you are pleased.

lines.text: Hello, Evans Lettings.
Hello, it's Megan from flat number six. I'm afraid the boiler has stopped working.
Oh dear. Is there any hot water?
No, nothing at all. And the radiators are completely cold.
That's not good, especially at this time of year. Have you checked the pressure?
Yes, it's very low. I've had a look, but I don't know how to fix it.
Don't worry. I'll ring the plumber and ask him to pop round this afternoon.
That would be brilliant. I'll be in until five.
Lovely. If he can't come today, I'll sort out an electric heater for you.
Thanks very much. Will I need to pay for the repair?
No, it's my responsibility. Cheers for letting me know, Megan.

sets.title: A day at the office
sets.intro: Listen to two coworkers in India. Notice words like prepone, revert and tiffin.
notes: The rhythm is often syllable-timed: each syllable has a similar length, so speech sounds even and fast.
The t and d sounds are often made with the tongue further back, and th can sound closer to t or d. This varies by speaker.
Stress can fall on different syllables than in British or American English.
Typical words: prepone (move earlier), do the needful (do what is needed), out of station, revert (reply), tiffin (lunch).
Speakers often put 'also' or 'only' at the end of a sentence for emphasis.

lines.text: Good morning, Neha. Did you get my mail about the meeting?
Yes, I did. Can we prepone it to ten o'clock? I have a call at noon.
Sure. I will do the needful and inform everyone.
Thank you. My manager is out of station this week, so he will revert next Monday.
No problem. Shall we have lunch together? I have brought my tiffin today.
Lovely. My mother made rice and dal. I will share some with you.
That sounds great. How do you come to the office?
I take the metro, then a rickshaw for the last part. It is quite cheap.
I drive, but the traffic is terrible. I should try the metro also.
Please do. It saves a lot of time.

sets.intro: Listen to a man visiting a flat that is for rent in India. Notice words like society, lift, maintenance and security deposit.
notes: People often say 'society' for a group of apartment buildings with shared rules and fees.

Good. And we can burn a few crackers in the compound with the children.
Only a few, na. The elders do not like too much noise.
Fine. I will keep it small and safe.

sets.intro: Words for family, friends and polite conversation in India. These words show respect and warmth.
notes: People often call older strangers 'uncle' or 'aunty' as a sign of respect, even when they are not related.
Family words are very specific: 'cousin brother' means a male cousin.

Speakers often add 'ji' after a name to be polite: 'Sharma ji'.

sets.title: Planning a braai
sets.intro: Listen to two friends planning a barbecue in South Africa. Notice braai, lekker, robot and just now.
notes: The short i in words like bit is often central, close to 'bet'. Speakers vary.
The r is often tapped or rolled lightly, and many words come from Afrikaans and Zulu.
'Ja' means yes. 'Eish' and 'shame' show surprise or sympathy.
Typical words: robot (traffic light), bakkie (pickup truck), braai (barbecue), lekker (nice), howzit (hello).
'Just now' means in a little while, and 'now-now' means very soon (but not always right now).

lines.text: Howzit, Emma! Are you coming to the braai on Saturday?
Ja, definitely. What time should I be there?
Around four. My dad is making the boerewors, and it is always lekker.
Sharp. Should I bring anything? Maybe some salad?
Salad is perfect. Can you also get ice? The shop closes at six, so go early.
Okay. I'll take my brother's bakkie, so I can carry everything.
Lekker. And watch out for the robot at the corner of Main Road. It's been broken since Monday.
Eish, that is bad. I will go the other way.
I'll phone you just now to check that you're okay.
Sharp sharp. See you on Saturday!

sets.title: Matric results
sets.intro: Listen to a student sharing her school exam results with her uncle in South Africa. Notice matric, varsity, bursary and stokvel.
notes: 'Matric' is both the last year of high school and the final exams.
'Varsity' is a friendly word for university.
Exclamations like 'hau' and 'yoh' show surprise or strong feelings.
'Ja no' is a common way to start a sentence that agrees.

lines.text: Uncle Sam, my matric results came out this morning!
Hau, already? Tell me, how did you do?
I passed with four distinctions, but I got only fifty percent for maths.
That is a very good result. Many learners struggle with maths.
I want to study medicine at varsity, but the fees are very high.
Have you looked for a bursary? Many companies offer one to top students.
Yes, I applied for two. They will tell me in January.
And your family stokvel can help with the books. Your mother told me about it.
Ja no, the stokvel has saved about twenty thousand rand this year.
That is wonderful. Your gogo will be so proud.

sets.title: Everyday expressions in South Africa
sets.intro: Short, lively expressions that South Africans use to show surprise, agree, say goodbye or have fun.
notes: Exclamations like 'yoh', 'hau' and 'sho' show surprise, and the tone changes the meaning.
'Sharp-sharp' is a friendly way to say okay or goodbye.
'Ja well no fine' is a long way of saying 'oh well, okay'.
'Ja' is yes, and 'ja no' often starts an answer that agrees.

learn.example: Yoh, that test was very difficult!

learn.def: a short word for surprise or disbelief (general English: oh, what)
learn.example: Hau, I did not expect so many people.

learn.def: a short word for surprise or for agreeing (general English: wow, okay)
learn.example: Sho, that was close!

learn.def: to have fun, or a party (general English: to party, to have fun)
learn.example: We are going to jol at the beach on Saturday.

learn.def: a friendly way to say okay or goodbye (general English: okay, bye)
learn.example: Sharp-sharp, I will call you tonight.

learn.def: a phrase for accepting something, like 'oh well' (general English: oh well, okay)
learn.example: The game is cancelled. Ja well no fine.

learn.def: a word for something cool or great (general English: cool, great)
learn.example: That new bike is really kief.

learn.def: a casual way to say goodbye (general English: see you later)
learn.example: I have to go now, check you later.

learn.def: a friendly way to agree or start an answer (general English: yes, exactly)
learn.example: Ja no, it was a long day.

learn.def: a sudden fright (general English: fright, scare)
learn.example: The loud noise gave me such a skrik.

learn.def: a word you say when something hurts (general English: ouch)
learn.example: Eina, that hurt my toe!

learn.def: just, or for no special reason (general English: just, simply)
learn.example: I sommer felt like going for a walk.
